**Evidence**
- SAFFIRE-I: To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew. [S1]
- SAFFIRE-I: First large-scale spacecraft fire experiment, run in a Cygnus cargo vehicle after it left the ISS: how fast a large fire grows in low gravity, and how low-g flammability compares with NASA's 1-g screening test. [S2]
- SAFFIRE-II: To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew. [S3]
- SAFFIRE-III: To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew. [S4]
- SAFFIRE-III: Repeat of the large-scale fabric fire in a Cygnus vehicle at 30 cm/s, in concurrent and opposed flow. [S5]

sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. sources.title: Microgravity and 1-g rankings of materials can disagree
sources.text: In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone samples (0.27–1.03 mm) had a burn length of about 0 in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while 2 of the 4 matching 1-g reference burns were complete. Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). Limitation: One test per configuration; single flow speed and near-normal O2.

sources.title: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative
sources.text: Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better in microgravity than in normal gravity. Limitation: Specific materials and geometries; flow and O2 per test partly only in raw files for BASS.

sources.title: Detectors must be checked against microgravity smoke, not Earth smoke
sources.text: SAME was designed around the hypothesis that, without buoyant flows, smoke particles from pyrolysing materials grow larger than in 1 g; SAME and SAME-R provide quantitative data on detector sensitivity to reduced-gravity smoke. Limitation: Pyrolysis (non-flaming) smoke; particle-size results are in reports/raw files, not in the summary table.

top_passage.text: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

top_passage.text: To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

top_passage.text: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.
